title: China Is Finding New Ways to Coerce Uyghurs Abroad
gist: A peer-reviewed study by the authors finds Beijing has shifted from overt transnational repression of the Uyghur diaspora toward 'restorative inducement' — conditional visits home to Xinjiang that first exploit a state-engineered separation from family, then extract informant recruitment, propaganda participation, or silence in exchange, a low-transgressiveness tactic that evades Western laws written for older, more visible forms of repression.

themes.theme: The scale and evolution of transnational repression

insights.claim: New Freedom House data show 54 governments — more than a quarter of the world's states — reached across borders to silence exiles and diaspora communities between 2014 and 2025, committing at least 1,375 direct, physical incidents across more than 100 host countries.
insights.speaker: Adrian Zenz, Muetter Tohti
insights.so_what: Quantifies the global scale of transnational repression as a systemic phenomenon rather than an isolated China-specific issue, relevant to human-rights and diaspora-security policy risk assessment.
insights.quote: 54 governments, more than a quarter of the world’s states, reached across borders to silence exiles and diaspora communities from 2014 to 2025, committing at least 1,375 direct, physical incidents in more than 100 host countries.
insights.locator: According to new data released by Freedom House

insights.claim: In 2025 the G-7 issued a joint statement on transnational repression and the European Parliament adopted a resolution targeting the issue, reflecting growing Western democratic institutional attention, even as the underlying threat is already evolving in form.
insights.speaker: Adrian Zenz, Muetter Tohti
insights.so_what: Signals rising institutional/regulatory attention that could translate into new Western legal instruments — relevant for tracking upcoming sanctions or legislative responses to transnational repression.
insights.quote: In 2025, the G-7 leaders issued a joint statement on the topic, and the European Parliament adopted a resolution on transnational repression targeting human rights defenders.
insights.locator: Western democracies are finally taking the threat seriously

insights.claim: The authors' framework, building on political scientist Johannes Gerschewski's 2013 theory that authoritarian stability rests on repression, co-optation, and legitimation, argues that the same three pillars now operate transnationally against diaspora communities — meaning repression alone is too narrow a concept to capture the modern threat.
insights.speaker: Adrian Zenz, Muetter Tohti
insights.so_what: Provides an analytical framework for anticipating that authoritarian states will increasingly pair coercion with 'soft' co-optation and propaganda tools that evade current transnational-repression legal definitions.
insights.quote: We argue that the same logic extends across borders. Regimes that perpetrate transnational repression also practice transnational co-optation, securing acquiescence by offering conditional benefits, as well as transnational legitimation
insights.locator: In 2013, the German political scientist Johannes Gerschewski

insights.claim: Since 2023 China has quietly, without formal announcement, opened Xinjiang's borders to visits by diaspora Uyghurs, a policy that spread by word of mouth and grew from a trickle of desperate individuals in 2024 to a normalized practice by 2025.
insights.speaker: Adrian Zenz, Muetter Tohti
insights.so_what: Documents a specific, dated policy shift by Beijing worth tracking as a template that other authoritarian states may adopt against their own diasporas.
insights.quote: Since 2023, the Chinese state has quietly opened Xinjiang’s borders to visits by diaspora Uyghurs. While never announced, the policy simply spread by word of mouth.
insights.locator: Beijing’s recent conduct toward the Uyghurs

insights.claim: The core mechanism the authors identify, termed 'restorative inducement,' works by having the state first engineer a deprivation — sealing Xinjiang off and detaining Uyghurs for receiving phone calls from abroad — and then offering to restore what it took, exploiting the resulting desperation.
insights.speaker: Adrian Zenz, Muetter Tohti
insights.so_what: A reusable analytical concept ('restorative inducement') for identifying similar coercive-then-benevolent tactics by other authoritarian regimes targeting diasporas.
insights.quote: The mechanism at this policy’s core is what our study calls a restorative inducement. The state first produced a deprivation. ... Then, having engineered the separation, the state offers to restore what it took.
insights.locator: The mechanism at this policy’s core

insights.claim: Interviews and leaked recordings describe Uyghurs traveling to Xinjiang in 2023-2024 being interrogated by police on arrival, with one Uyghur American man offered jobs, business funding, and travel permits in exchange for becoming an informant on Uyghur communities abroad, and threatened with his parents being sent to a reeducation camp when he hesitated.
insights.speaker: Adrian Zenz, Muetter Tohti
insights.so_what: A concrete case illustrating the coercive recruitment mechanism operating beneath the surface of the ostensibly benign 'family visit' policy — relevant to due-diligence and security assessments for diaspora-linked individuals or organizations.
insights.quote: “In return, we want you to be our informant,” officials told him. “If there is anything that grabs your attention in the Uyghur communities abroad, we want to be informed about that. ... If you cooperate well with us, we can also help to send your parents and your younger sister to you.”
insights.locator: In confidential interviews and leaked recordings

insights.claim: Some visitors are conscripted into propaganda upon return, with one visitor videotaped delivering a scripted statement that 'Uyghurs are doing well, and Xinjiang is booming,' while feeling compelled to maintain contact with police afterward for fear the recording could be used to brand her a traitor in her own community.
insights.speaker: Adrian Zenz, Muetter Tohti
insights.so_what: Shows how China converts individual coercion into ongoing propaganda content that can shape international perception of conditions in Xinjiang.
insights.quote: Another visitor was videotaped delivering a scripted statement declaring that “Uyghurs are doing well, and Xinjiang is booming.”

insights.claim: Not all visits end safely: earlier in 2026 an Istanbul-based Uyghur who had joined four state-organized tours was detained on a subsequent private visit to Xinjiang and sentenced to six years in prison.
insights.speaker: Adrian Zenz, Muetter Tohti
insights.so_what: Demonstrates that the visa/visit policy carries real, unpredictable risk even for those who had previously traveled without incident — a caution against assuming the program is safe based on prior experience.
insights.quote: Yet others fare far worse: Earlier this year, one Istanbul-based Uyghur who had joined four state-organized tours was detained on a private visit and sentenced to six years in prison.

themes.theme: Effects on the diaspora and the concept of transgressiveness

insights.claim: Beijing's strategy of transnational co-optation is succeeding where years of overt threats did not: as more travelers returned apparently unscathed, Uyghur communities' risk perception shifted, silence became a reasonable price for family reunification, and participation in protests and advocacy has declined precipitously.
insights.speaker: Adrian Zenz, Muetter Tohti
insights.so_what: Demonstrates a measurable chilling effect on diaspora activism as a direct outcome of the visa-based inducement policy, relevant to assessing the durability of exile advocacy movements against Beijing.
insights.quote: After more travelers came home apparently unscathed, the risk perception of Uyghur communities shifted. ... As a result, participation in protests and advocacy has declined precipitously.

insights.claim: The Uyghur Transitional Justice Database, which once collected 40 to 50 testimonies per research trip, has recently struggled to secure even five, illustrating a sharp decline in the availability of firsthand testimony documenting Xinjiang abuses.
insights.speaker: Adrian Zenz, Muetter Tohti
insights.so_what: A quantified, concrete indicator of the co-optation policy's chilling effect on documentation efforts — implies future human-rights reporting on Xinjiang may become significantly harder to source and verify.
insights.quote: Where earlier research trips by the Uyghur Transitional Justice Database yielded 40 to 50 testimonies, the organization’s team recently struggled to secure five.
insights.locator: Witnesses withdraw their testimonies or fall silent

insights.claim: The authors introduce the concept of 'transgressiveness' — the degree to which a tactic violates host-country laws and international norms — arguing Beijing deliberately favors tactics like conditional family visits that are low in transgressiveness (breaking no law in Washington or Berlin) yet high in behavioral impact, unlike high-transgressiveness tactics such as assassinations that invite prosecution and global attention.
insights.speaker: Adrian Zenz, Muetter Tohti
insights.so_what: A key analytical tool for predicting which forms of authoritarian transnational coercion will proliferate: low-transgressiveness tactics are more scalable and legally invulnerable than overt violence.
insights.quote: Beijing’s adapted strategy deliberately favors tactics that are low in transgressiveness yet high in impact.

insights.claim: Because a conditional family visit breaks no law in Washington or Berlin, while an assassination is highly transgressive and invites prosecution, current Western legal frameworks against transnational repression — calibrated for the more visible, older tactics — remain structurally inadequate against these lower-transgressiveness innovations.
insights.speaker: Adrian Zenz, Muetter Tohti
insights.so_what: Directly warns policymakers that current or pending Western transnational-repression legislation may be obsolete on arrival, a call to action for legal/regulatory reform relevant to human-rights and diaspora-protection policy.
insights.quote: instruments calibrated to yesterday’s tactics will remain inadequate against adversaries who innovate faster than democracies legislate. The gravest incidents in transnational repression next year may well be the ones that never appear in any report.
insights.locator: An advantage of tactics that are low

insights.claim: Beijing's Xinjiang image campaign follows Xi Jinping's 2022 order to officials to 'tell the story of China's Xinjiang well,' exemplified by January 2026 state media coverage of 42 Xinjiang-born Turkish residents brought on a homeland tour organized by the Chinese consulate and the CCP's United Front Work Department.
insights.speaker: Adrian Zenz, Muetter Tohti
insights.so_what: Ties the coercive visit program to a broader, top-down state image-management campaign directed by Xi Jinping himself, contextualizing it as coordinated policy rather than a local initiative.
insights.quote: Beijing has poured resources into rehabilitating Xinjiang’s image ever since Chinese leader Xi Jinping ordered officials in 2022 to “tell the story of China’s Xinjiang well.”

insights.claim: China's evolving model exemplifies what scholars Sergei Guriev and Daniel Treisman call 'spin dictatorship' — rulers who prefer the quiet engineering of perceptions over visible terror, making Beijing's open-door tactic look like normalization to an unsuspecting outsider.
insights.speaker: Adrian Zenz, Muetter Tohti
insights.so_what: Places China's Uyghur policy within a recognized academic model of modern authoritarian governance, useful for comparative analysis with other 'spin dictatorships.'
insights.quote: This is repression for the age of what the scholars Sergei Guriev and Daniel Treisman call “spin dictators”: rulers who prefer the quiet engineering of perceptions to visible terror.

insights.claim: Other authoritarian states are adopting similar conditional-access tools: Eritrea conditions consular services and property rights on a diaspora tax and political quiescence; Belarus's 2023 return commission extracts pro-regime statements and intelligence from returning exiles; Assad's Syria conditioned refugee return on security clearances used to compel informing on relatives; and Rwanda courts its diaspora with homeland tours and civic education camps.
insights.speaker: Adrian Zenz, Muetter Tohti
insights.so_what: Demonstrates that conditional-homeland-access as a co-optation tool is a spreading, multi-country authoritarian pattern rather than a China-specific tactic, broadening the scope of diaspora-security risk assessment beyond the Uyghur case.
insights.quote: Eritrea has conditioned its consular services and property rights at home on payment of a diaspora tax and on political quiescence. In 2023, Belarus created a new commission through which exiles could petition to return safely after “repenting”
